title: Grammar Terms: Modal Verbs and Clauses
keyIdea: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must) help a main verb and show how sure or how able we are: might and could are possible, should is likely, will and must are certain. Adverbs such as perhaps and surely also show possibility, but they are not verbs. A relative clause adds detail about a noun and starts with who, which, where, when, whose or that. A parenthesis is extra information inside commas, brackets or dashes; lift it out and the sentence still works.

kid: Some verbs are helpers. They sit before the main verb and tell us how sure we are. These helpers are called modal verbs. It might rain means it is possible. It should rain means it is likely. It will rain means it is certain. Must is strong too: you must wear a seatbelt.
Can, could, may, would and shall are modal verbs as well. Words like maybe and perhaps show how sure we are, but they are adverbs, not verbs.
A relative clause adds detail about a noun. The girl who won the race is my sister. Use who for people, which for things and where for places.
A parenthesis is extra information. My dog, a cheeky terrier, ate my sock. Take out a cheeky terrier and the sentence still works. Put commas, brackets or dashes round it.
adult: This is Year 5 grammar in the English national curriculum (Appendix 2). Children show degrees of possibility with modal verbs, such as might, should, will and must, or with adverbs, such as perhaps and surely. They write relative clauses that begin with who, which, where, when, whose or that, or with the relative pronoun left out. They use brackets, dashes or commas to mark parenthesis, and commas to make meaning clear or to avoid ambiguity. They also build cohesion in a paragraph with words like then, after that and this.

The terms children must know are modal verb, relative pronoun, relative clause, parenthesis, bracket, dash, cohesion and ambiguity. A modal verb never changes for the subject: she can, not she cans. It is followed by the plain form of the main verb: you should go. Modal verbs can also show ability (can), permission (may) or duty (must), not just how likely something is.

Common mistakes: calling maybe or perhaps a modal verb, when they are adverbs; forgetting that can and would are modals; using which for people (the man which); and writing should of for should have. With parenthesis, a frequent slip is putting a comma before the extra part but not after it. Children also think parenthesis only means brackets. Ask them to lift the part out and read what is left.

In the lab your child drags modal verbs onto a possible, likely or certain scale. They turn a dial until the modal matches a weather forecast. They tap the modal verb in a sentence that has maybe as a trap. They drop who, which or where into a relative clause, and they lift out a parenthesis to prove the sentence still works.

familyTip: Watch a weather forecast together and turn it into modal sentences: at 20% it might rain, at 90% it will probably rain. Then ask your child to add a parenthesis to one sentence about the weather.

visual.caption: Possible or certain? Drag each word to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: place modal verbs on a certainty scale, match a dial to the forecast, spot the modal verb, fill relative clauses and lift out a parenthesis.

practice.prompt: Which sentence is the most certain?
practice.hint: Put might, could and will on a scale from possible to certain.
practice.explain: Will is certain. Might and could only say that winning is possible.

practice.prompt: A sentence has {n} words. Only one of them is a modal verb. How many words are not modal verbs?
practice.hint: Take the one modal verb away from the {n} words.
practice.explain: {n} words take away 1 modal verb leaves {=n-1} words. A sentence usually has just one modal, right before the main verb.

practice.prompt: Pick the right word: The man ___ lives next door has a parrot.
practice.hint: Is the man a person, a thing or a place?
practice.explain: Who is for people, so it starts this relative clause. Which is for things and where is for places.

practice.prompt: You write {n} sentences. Each one has a parenthesis inside commas, like My dog, a cheeky terrier, ate my sock. How many commas do you use?
practice.hint: A parenthesis in commas needs one comma before it and one after it.
practice.explain: Each parenthesis needs 2 commas, so {n} sentences need {=2*n} commas. A common slip is to leave off the second one.

pool.prompt: Which word is a modal verb?
pool.hint: A modal verb helps a main verb, as in you ___ go.
pool.explain: Should is a modal verb: you should go. Perhaps and quickly are adverbs.

pool.prompt: Which is the parenthesis? Our teacher, Ms Cole, loves maps.
pool.hint: Lift each part out. Which one leaves a sentence that still works?
pool.explain: Lift out Ms Cole and you get Our teacher loves maps, which still works. So Ms Cole is the parenthesis.

pool.hint: Say it slowly. The word after should is have, even if it sounds like of.
pool.explain: Should have is right. Should of is a common slip because should've sounds like should of.

pool.prompt: The forecast says a 10% chance of snow. Which sentence fits best?
pool.hint: 10% is a small chance. Which modal is weakest?
pool.explain: A small chance needs a weak modal, so it might snow. Will and must would sound certain.

pool.prompt: Which word starts a relative clause about a place?
pool.hint: This is the park ___ we play. Which word means at that place?
pool.explain: Where is for places: this is the park where we play. Who is for people and whose shows belonging.

pool.prompt: Your paragraph uses {n} modal verbs and {k} adverbs such as perhaps and surely. How many of these words are verbs?
pool.hint: Perhaps and surely show possibility, but are they verbs?
pool.explain: Only the {n} modal verbs are verbs. The {k} adverbs show possibility too, but they are not verbs.

pool.prompt: You write {n} sentences, each with a parenthesis in brackets. How many brackets do you type?
pool.hint: Each parenthesis needs an opening bracket and a closing bracket.
pool.explain: Each one needs 2 brackets, so {n} sentences need {=2*n} brackets.

pool.prompt: I saw the man with the telescope. Why is this sentence ambiguous?
pool.hint: Who has the telescope? Could it be either person?
pool.explain: It is ambiguous: either you used the telescope, or the man had it. Rewording can make the meaning clear.
